activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Homesickness is the distress of being away from home and familiar people; it is common after a move and usually eases as a person settles in.
story:
Bennett stood in Willa's garage, which her dad had strung with paper lanterns for the farewell party, and tried to memorize everything at once. The folding table with the dented punch bowl. Alden attempting to juggle three dinner rolls and failing gloriously. He was leaving in six days, and he had a theory that if he collected enough of this, packed it in his head like souvenirs, the move would hurt less.

Willa slid next to him by the chip bags. "You're doing the staring thing," she said. "You did it at the science fair too, right before your volcano won."

"I'm recruiting memories," Bennett said. "For the move."

Willa frowned, which meant she was actually thinking. "That's backwards. When we moved here in fourth grade, I cried at a photo of my old street for like a month. Homesickness, my mom called it. Being away from home and all your familiar people." She grabbed a chip. "It didn't stop until I got used to things here. You can't stockpile against it, it just... happens, and then it fades while you settle in. My mom said it's really common, like almost everybody gets it."

Bennett didn't want to believe her. He'd been feeling quietly rebellious about the whole move anyway, refusing to pack his bookshelf, and part of him felt a smoldering resentment toward his dad's new job, even though his dad hadn't done anything wrong exactly. If Willa was right, then his memory-collecting was pointless, like bringing an umbrella to stop it from raining. He decided to test it. He closed his eyes for ten whole seconds in the middle of the party and tried to burn the garage into his brain. When he opened them, Alden had stacked all the dinner rolls into a wobbly pyramid on Bennett's head.

"Science," Alden said solemnly.

Bennett laughed so hard the rolls cascaded onto his shoes, and Mr. Mwangi from next door poked his head in, saw the rolls, and quietly added one more to the pile before anyone could stop him.

Later, when the lanterns were being taken down, Bennett thought about a choice he'd made back in fourth grade, before Willa arrived. There had been another new kid that year, a quiet boy who ate alone, and Bennett had never sat with him. He'd told himself the boy seemed fine. Now he wondered. Had that kid gone home and cried over some street he missed, while Bennett, who could have helped, just watched?

He found Willa pulling a lantern off its string. "When I get there," he said, "I'm going to find whoever eats alone. Just so you know. That's my plan."

"Recruit them into your pyramid of science?" she said.

"Obviously."

She handed him the lantern, the green one, still warm from its bulb. "Take it. Put it in your new room."

He held it by its wire loop, careful, like it might remember this night as long as he did.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Hypotheses are often written as 'If ..., then ...' statements, which name the change being made and the result that is predicted.
story:
Eva had exactly forty minutes before the judges reached her table, and her bean plants were acting strange. Two weeks ago she had started them for her project, and one pot by the window had sprouted tall and green while the other, on the shelf by the door, sat there doing basically nothing. The whole fair buzzed around her in the gym: a kid named Brogan was testing whether his polymer balls could bounce higher off concrete than off carpet, and Channing was trying to negotiate a second extension from Mr. Sadeghi because her volcano kept leaking. Eva waved them both over.

"Look at these," Eva said, pointing at the pots. "Same seeds, same water, same soil. So why is this one winning?"

Brogan leaned in until his nose almost touched the leaves. "Maybe it likes you better. Plants can sense stuff."

"Plants can't sense stuff."

"Then explain the window pot, genius."

Channing peered at both pots, then at the poster Eva had propped up, which read, in giant hopeful letters, PLANTS LIKE MUSIC. "Wait," she said. "What does that even mean? How would you know if a plant likes music? It can't clap."

Eva opened her mouth, then closed it. Her poster had a nice drawing and a title she'd made at eleven o'clock the night before, and absolutely nothing else. A judge with a clipboard was already circling nearer, pausing at each table, and the clock above the bleachers showed thirty-one minutes.

"Mr. Sadeghi," Channing announced, and dragged him over before Eva could stop her. He read the poster, then looked at Eva with the mild smile that meant trouble.

"Interesting claim," he said. "Tell me, how would you test it?"

Eva's mind went blank, then scrambled. Test it. A plant couldn't say yes or no, so you had to make it show you somehow. "You could play music for one plant and not another," she said slowly, "and then see if they grow differently."

"Better. But what exactly will you look for? Guess what will happen first, in one sentence."

Eva stared at the pots. A guess you could actually check. "If I play music for one plant and not the other, then... the music plant will grow taller." She said it out loud and felt something click into place. "That's a real hypothesis. If, then. The change, and what I predict."

Mr. Sadeghi nodded once and moved on, but Eva wasn't done, because the shelf plant still made no sense, and now she had a tool. If light were the difference, then moving the shelf plant to the window should fix it. She carried the pot over, set it beside its rival, and marked both with tape labels so no judge could accuse her of cheating.

At the twenty-minute mark, Brogan wandered back holding one of his polymer balls, which had somehow gotten stuck in his hair. "Your hypothesis has a problem," he said, chewing gum with great seriousness. "I watered your shelf plant Tuesday. With soda. It looked thirsty and I felt bad."

Eva grabbed his sleeve. "How much soda?"

"Like half a can. It was orange."

So there was her hidden cause, sitting there the whole time, sweet and orange and patient. She yanked a fresh poster board from under the table and wrote fast: her if-then sentence, the shelf plant, the soda confession signed by a guilty witness. When the judge finally stopped at her table, Eva pointed at the tall pot, the struggling one, and Brogan, who raised his hand like he was swearing on a Bible.

"The data," she said, "is durable. The witness, less so."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, is marked by lighting small oil lamps called diyas and is usually celebrated over five days.
story:
Liam arrived at the street festival just after four o'clock, carrying a box of small clay lamps his grandmother had sent. He was supposed to set them up at the community table, but when he got there, the organizer pointed at the sky and said the lamps had to be burning before dark, and dark came at six. Liam had about forty lamps and one strip of ledge along the festival stage to work with.

Archie and Marissa found him counting lamps out of the box. "What are those?" Archie asked.

"They're called diyas," Liam said. "Little oil lamps. You light them for Diwali, the festival of lights." He held one up so they could see the shallow bowl and the cotton wick lying inside.

Marissa picked up a lamp and turned it over. "You need oil for all of these? We have two hours."

"There's a jug behind the stage," Liam said. "But if we pour one at a time, we'll never make it." He thought about the problem. Instead of filling lamps one by one, they could coordinate the jobs: one person poured oil, one placed wicks, one carried finished lamps to the ledge and spaced them out. He told Archie and Marissa the plan, and they set up an assembly line on the folding table, moving the lamps left to right like cars through a car wash.

They had filled about thirty when a man from the next booth complained that the lamps were too close to his stall. The festival organizer came over, looking like a judge about to rule on a case, and Marissa whispered, "You'd better argue well, defendant." The man said fire near his paper decorations wasn't safe, and Liam pointed out that the ledge ran along the stage, not the booth. The organizer measured the gap with his arm, said it was fine, and told the man to move his decorations back a foot.

By ten to six, the last lamp sat on the ledge, and a woman from the temple went along the row with a long match, tipping each flame alive. As the sky turned grey, the diyas glowed one after another, a bright line against the darkening street. Liam's grandmother had told him on the phone that this was only the first night, and that the festival would go on for five days, with the lamps lit again each evening. He would come back tomorrow, and the day after, with the same box.

"Look at that," Archie said, and pointed to where a little girl in a gold dress was holding her hands near the flames, not touching, just feeling the warmth.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see.
story:
Joseph sat on Martha's kitchen floor with her phone balanced on his knee, scrolling through photos from Saturday's soccer game while Martha microwaved popcorn in the next room. He stopped at a picture of himself mid-jump, mouth open, eyes crossed, looking like a startled frog. He had never seen it before. Martha's account was private, he knew that, because she'd made a big deal of it last month. Only followers could see her posts, and she'd bragged that she'd counted every one of them.

"Martha," he called. "When did you take this?"

She came in shaking a bag of popcorn. "Saturday. Why?"

"It has forty likes." He held up the phone. "You have like thirty followers."

Martha frowned and took the phone. She tapped the picture, scrolled, and her eyebrows went up. The likes kept loading. Then she opened her messages, and there it was: her private post, forwarded by a boy named Dylan from another school, sent to a group chat with eighty people in it. "I didn't even know Dylan followed me," she said slowly. "I accepted him forever ago because he commented on my cat video."

Joseph leaned over her shoulder. "So being private doesn't matter?"

"It limits who sees my posts," Martha said. "But anyone I already accepted can still copy or share what they see." She said it like she was reading it off a wall, and Joseph could tell she'd just figured it out too.

He thought about that while she chewed popcorn. He had his own account, also private, with a follower named Catherine from summer camp, a girl he'd spoken to exactly twice. If she could forward anything he posted, then his embarrassing trip-and-fall video from the pool party last week wasn't as safe as he'd believed. He borrowed Martha's phone to check, since his own was dead at home, and yes, there was Catherine, still on his list, still able to see everything.

"What are you doing?" Martha asked.

"Testing something." He went to his page through her account, saved the pool party video to her camera roll with a few taps, and then deleted it. The copy stayed in the photos. That was the part that made his stomach drop. Even if he deleted a post, anyone could have already saved it, and he would never know. He showed Martha the saved video sitting there on her phone like evidence.

"So what do we do?" she asked.

Joseph made her go through her followers one by one, unfollowing anyone she couldn't actually name. When she got to Dylan, she hesitated, then pressed remove. He did the same thing later at home, starting with Catherine. It seemed plausible that most of his followers were fine, but "seemed plausible" wasn't the same as knowing, so he checked each one anyway.

On Monday, a kid from Mr. Ramos's homeroom stopped Joseph in the hall and grinned. "Nice frog face," the kid said. Joseph just looked at him and kept walking. At lunch, Martha slid her phone across the table, showing him she'd made a new account. "Private from day one," she said. "And this time I know every follower's actual face."

"Show me how you set it up," Joseph said, and pulled out his phone.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: In a blind test, participants do not know which sample is which, so their expectations cannot sway their answers.
story:
Jace spread his notebook across the library table and wrote, in careful letters, "Does the brand name change how cereal tastes?" His project for the science fair was due in nine days, and so far all he had was a question and two boxes of corn flakes in his backpack, one famous and expensive, one from the store's own shelf. He had asked Audrey and Anaya to meet him in the back corner by the biography section, because the librarian let you talk there as long as you whispered.

"Here's the problem," Jace said when they arrived. "If you hand people a bowl and tell them it's the fancy brand, they'll probably say it's better. That's not really a taste test. That's a test of the box." Audrey frowned at the two boxes poking out of his bag. "So don't show them the boxes," she said. "Hide them. Pour the cereal, label the bowls A and B, and don't tell anyone which is which." Anaya tapped the table. "Then nobody's expectations can sway their answers. It's called a blind test. My sister did one for her project last year." Jace wrote it down fast, feeling the shape of a real experiment forming at last.

They set up right there. Audrey took both boxes behind the study carrel, out of everyone's sight, and came back with two unlabeled bags. She filled six bowls, marked A on three and B on three, and shuffled their positions when Jace wasn't looking. Anaya fetched water cups. One by one, they tasted, rinsed, and wrote their scores on slips of paper that Jace folded without reading. A man at the next table watched them crunching and whispering, and once the librarian drifted over, but she only raised an eyebrow and moved on.

Jace unfolded the slips at home that night, and his stomach dropped. Six out of six picks favored bowl B. He stared at the pile, sure he had messed something up, because B had to be the cheap one. He was certain of it. Certain, that is, until he opened his backpack and found a folded note tucked into the famous brand's box.

"Dear detective," the note read, in Audrey's looping handwriting. "You checked my bags twice but never the boxes. I swapped the cereal before you even got to the library. The flakes in the famous box came from the store-brand bag. Your labels were never right, and that's the twist for your board: if you can't trust the box, how can you trust your tongue? Bring eight dollars to lunch. I had to buy both bags. Audrey."

He laughed out loud in his dark kitchen. His first experiment had failed in the most useful way possible, and that insight was better than any result: the labels themselves could lie. He would need a more sophisticated setup for the fair, numbered samples, sealed envelopes, someone else holding the key. He sat back down, opened his notebook to a fresh page, and began writing the story of how bowl B won.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Knowing a word's language of origin can help with spelling: the 'k' sound in 'chorus' is spelled 'ch' because it comes from Greek, while the 'sh' in 'chef' comes from French.
story:
The spelling bee was down to three people, and Aiden wanted the dictionary that Mr. Cardinal kept on his desk, the big one with the ribbon bookmarks, promised to the winner. Marko had spelled "prohibit" without pausing, and Leela, who wanted the trophy that came with the dictionary more than she wanted the dictionary itself, had gotten through "fungus" and "extravagant." Now it was Aiden's turn.

"Chorus," said Mr. Cardinal. "Language of origin: Greek."

Aiden stared at the chalkboard behind Mr. Cardinal's head. The k sound. He thought about the word list he'd studied with his mother, where he'd tripped over "chef" twice. Chef had the sh sound spelled c-h, and next to it in the notes his mother had written "French." Chef was French, and it used c-h for the sh sound. If French used c-h for sh, then Greek might use c-h for the k sound. He had never seen it written down; he was guessing from the pattern.

"C-h-o-r-u-s," he said. "Chorus."

"Correct," said Mr. Cardinal.

Leela clapped once, then pressed her hands flat on her desk. Her word was "chef." She asked for the language of origin, the way spellers did, and Mr. Cardinal said, "French." Aiden watched her mouth move. She started with c, then hesitated, changed it, and said "s-h-e-f." The bell on Mr. Cardinal's desk rang.

Marko went out on "chaos," trying s-h at the front, so it was Aiden and Leela. She got "chimney" right, glaring at the ceiling while she spelled it. Then Aiden had "orchestra." Greek again, Mr. Cardinal said. The k sound after the vowel. If the pattern held, it was c-h here too.

"O-r-c-h-e-s-t-r-a," Aiden said. "Orchestra."

"Correct," said Mr. Cardinal. "One more. Leela, 'chef.'"

She closed her eyes. "C-h-e-f. Chef."

"Correct," Mr. Cardinal said, and wrote both their names on the board side by side. "We'll settle it Monday." He slid the dictionary an inch toward the center of the desk. Leela leaned over and touched the cover, once, like she was checking it would still be there.

"Chorus," she said to Aiden on the way out. "I never would have tried c-h."

"Chef," Aiden said. "You almost lost it and you didn't."

She pulled the trophy off the shelf by the window and held it up so he could see his reflection in the bowl of it. "Monday," she said. "Bring your pattern."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed.
story:
The family group chat, which was called FAM JAM because his uncle thought he was funny, lit up at 4:32 on Friday afternoon, and Eli grabbed his phone off the bus seat like it was on fire.

"First dance TONIGHT," he typed. "I cannot dance. This is an emergency."

His mom answered first with seventeen exclamation points. His dad sent a thumbs up, which helped nobody. Then his grandmother, who had learned to send videos that spring, dropped in a clip of a white bird with a yellow crest bobbing its head, stomping, and swinging its neck in perfect time while a pop song played. Eli watched it four times. Under the video his grandmother had typed, "If this bird can do it, so can you."

Eli read the caption next to the video twice. In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel had shown that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed. He sat up so fast he banged his head on the bus window. The bird didn't just bounce around. It kept the beat, and when the beat slowed down or sped up, the bird slowed down or sped up with it. He screen-recorded the clip and forwarded it to Kade and then, after a long minute of deciding, to Sia, because Sia had told him at lunch that she was "probably just going to stand near the punch" and had said it while looking at her tray like it might save her.

"Scientific proof that rhythm is learnable," Eli texted. "This bird changed speed when the song changed speed. It adjusted. It ADJUSTED, Sia."

Kade replied with "lol" and then, a minute later, "wait that's actually kind of great."

Sia sent one message back: "A bird. Really."

At the dance, the gym smelled like floor wax and the banner hung perpendicular to the wall, sagging a little in the middle, and the DJ was terrible in the best possible way. Eli and Sia stood near the punch for two whole songs, and then the speakers switched to something slow at first and then quicker. Sia tilted her head. "Okay," she said. "Tempo change. If the bird can adjust, I can adjust." She started small, just shifting her weight, then matched it when the song sped up, and Eli matched her, and it worked, it actually worked, and Kade spun past doing a move that made him look like a startled kangaroo, some kind of bouncing marsupial, and Sia laughed so hard she nearly stopped dancing but didn't.

Later there was a brief argument about whose fault it was that Kade's elbow had knocked two cups of punch onto the floor, and Eli mediated by declaring that both of them had to help the coach mop, which they did, still keeping time to the music.

In the bathroom mirror, holding his phone at a careful angle, Eli took a photo of his sweaty, grinning face and sent it to FAM JAM with one word: "Snowball."

His grandmother replied in under a minute. "That's my boy."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Typing a message in all capital letters is widely read as shouting in online communication.
story:
The Saturday skate session was Nolan's whole plan for the weekend, and at 9:04 a.m. he opened the group chat to confirm it. Three messages sat there already. Kellen had written, "meet at the park at ten?" Ludovik had replied with a thumbs up and a photo of his board with new wheels. Nolan typed, "I'll be there" and then, worried his plain little message would get buried before anyone read it, deleted it and typed again in capitals: I WILL BE THERE.

Ludovik answered within a minute. "why are you yelling?" Nolan stared at the screen. Yelling? He had been sitting silently on his bed, not making a sound. He typed, "I'm not yelling, I'm at home," and Ludovik sent a single laughing emoji, then, "all caps = shouting, everyone knows that." Kellen added, "you sounded like a coach blowing the whistle, lol."

Nolan set the phone down and walked to the window, thinking it over. So the letters themselves carried a voice. He scrolled back through weeks of messages, testing the idea against the evidence, and found a pattern: whenever Ludovik's mother made him log off, his last message was always something like "I HAVE TO GO." Those messages did read like shouts, even though Nolan had never pictured it before. Mr. Banerjee from next door had once sent a notice to the whole street email list about the parking rules, all in capitals, and three people had written back sounding offended before he apologized and sent it again in lowercase. Same words, different letters, different feeling. It was like a principle of some kind, hidden inside the typing itself.

Still, part of Nolan opposed the whole idea. He had used capitals just to be noticed, not to be loud, and nobody had asked him that. He felt hesitant about typing anything else now, in case he got it wrong twice in one morning. He decided on a test. He sent a private message, just to Kellen: "in caps i meant please see my message. was that annoying?" Kellen replied, "kind of, yeah, but it's fine. just use regular letters, people will see it."

Nolan typed, "ok. see you at ten. bringing the ramp." Then he paused, and added one more line in the group chat, in careful lowercase: "sorry for shouting at you guys." Ludovik sent back, "we forgive you, don't do it at the park or the little kids will cry." Nolan grabbed his helmet and shoved the phone in his pocket, already out the door and halfway down the stairs.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing.
story:
The swim team had a problem, and it had a name that Henry didn't know yet. For the first three weeks of the season, the relay squad did nothing but argue. Abygael insisted the backstroke swimmer should go second. Megan wanted the fastest kid to anchor, even though that was Henry's spot, and she said so at every practice in the indoor pool behind the community centre. The water in the shallow end seemed to fluctuate between calm and chaos depending on who was yelling loudest on the deck.

Henry wanted that anchor leg more than he wanted almost anything. But he also wanted the relay to stop falling apart, because at the end of the month there was a real meet, and a team that fought at the wall would fight at the handoff too. He started paying attention, not to the arguments themselves but to the pattern underneath them. Week one, everyone had been shy and polite, learning names, copying the older swimmers. Week two, the politeness cracked open. Week three, the fighting felt almost organized, like it was settling into lanes.

He mentioned it to Mr. Tesfaye, who ran the pool and lived as a tenant in the apartment upstairs, coming down most evenings to check the chlorine. "It's like the team has stages," Henry said, dragging the kickboard back to the rack. "First everyone's nice, then everyone fights, then maybe something else."

Mr. Tesfaye smiled and said only, "There's a book in the lost-and-found box that might interest you. Nobody's claimed it since autumn." He did not say anything more, which was typical of him.

The book was a fat paperback about how groups work, and Henry found the page that night at his kitchen table. Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing. He read it three times. The next morning at school he showed Megan the page. "See? Forming, storming, norming and performing," he said. "We're in the storming part. It's supposed to happen. The fighting isn't the end, it's a stage."

Megan squinted at it. "So if it's a stage, we just have to get through it?"

"That's my idea," Henry said. "But it won't just be time. We have to make the norming part happen. Mr. Tesfaye says the pool temperature is cumulative, little changes adding up all day. I think trust works like that too. Small things, stacked."

So at the next practice Henry stopped defending his lane and started stacking. When Abygael fumbled her goggles, he fished them off the bottom before she even finished her lap. When Megan's split time was bad, he told her what was good about her turn instead. Megan, who secretly wanted to be the one organizing everybody, grabbed the whiteboard from the office and drew the order of the relay, then handed the marker to Abygael. "You decide the backstroke spot," Megan said. Abygael wrote her own name second, and nobody argued.

At the meet, their handoffs were clean, one after another, and when Henry touched the wall at the end of the anchor leg, Megan was already reaching down to pull him out. "Told you," she said, grinning at the scoreboard. "Norming."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Coping means the ways a person handles stress or difficult feelings; healthy coping strategies include exercise, getting enough sleep and talking with someone trusted.
story:
Olivier had noticed a pattern. On the nights before a math test, his stomach hurt, and on test mornings it hurt again. He had started keeping track on the back of his planner, and the bad-stomach days correspond exactly with quiz days. So it was not the cafeteria food, and it was not a virus. Something invisible was going on, and he wanted to know what.

He mentioned it to Calista while they were fighting with his locker, which had become rebellious lately and refused to open on the first three tries. "Does your stomach hurt before tests?" he asked. "Or is that just me?"

Calista got the locker open on the fourth yank. "Not my stomach. My brain does this loop where I imagine every way I could fail." She shrugged. "My mom calls it anxiety. She says everyone gets it, some people just get it louder."

That word rang a small bell. Mr. Ferreira had used it in homeroom last week, in the middle of a lesson on extinction, of all things. He had been explaining why the passenger pigeon died out, then paused and said some students had looked anxious about the science fair, and that anxiety was a normal response to stress. Olivier had mostly been drawing a pigeon at the time. Now he wished he had listened better.

So he ran a test of his own, the way he would test any rule. Thursday was the unit test, and on Wednesday night he did three things differently: he went for a bike ride around the block twice, he got in bed an hour earlier than usual, and he told his dad the whole thing, even the part about the planner chart. His dad didn't solve anything, he mostly listened and said the chart was smart. Thursday morning Olivier's stomach was quiet.

At lunch he found Calista and Rafael at the far table. "It worked," he said, sitting down. "Exercise, extra sleep, and talking to my dad. No stomach ache."

Rafael looked up from his tray. "Wait, what works?"

"Coping," Olivier said. "It means the ways you handle stress. I always thought it just meant, like, surviving. But there are actual strategies, and you can test them like a science experiment." He tore his chicken sandwich in half and offered a piece to Rafael.

"Next time I loop," Calista said, "I'm telling my mom instead of staring at my ceiling."

"Eleven tonight," Rafael said. "Basketball at my driveway. Bring the ball, mine's flat."

Olivier pointed at Rafael's tray. "Deal. Now eat your green beans."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: A ball that rolls 3 meters in 2 seconds has an average speed of 1.5 meters per second.
story:
Cole had thought the ball was moving fast, but the numbers said otherwise. He had watched Emerson bowl an old soccer ball down the flat concrete channel between the ramps at the skate park, and it had looked quick, so quick that his first guess at its speed had been way off. Now he crouched at the top of the channel with a tape measure in one hand and his phone stopwatch in the other, because Mr. Vargas's science assignment was due Monday, and the assignment asked for a distance-time graph of something that rolled.

"You're doing homework at a skate park," Anis said, rolling up beside them on his board.

"I'm doing homework on you guys," Cole said. "I need a ball, a distance, and a time. The graph I can draw at home."

He stretched the tape along the channel and marked three meters with a scrap of chalk. Three meters, no more, no less, because a short negotiation with Emerson had settled it: Emerson wanted a longer run so the ball would speed up on the slope, but Cole needed a flat, measured stretch or his graph would be wrong before he started. Emerson had finally agreed it was more feasible to roll on the flat and keep the measurement honest.

"Start it when I say go," Cole said. He crouched at the chalk line. "Not before, not after. Exactly on go."

Emerson set the ball down and steadied it. Anis leaned on his board to watch. Mr. Vargas, who had come down to the park with his dog, stopped near the fence but said nothing, which suited Cole fine.

"Go."

Emerson released the ball. Cole's thumb hit the stopwatch the instant it crossed the chalk line, and he watched it travel, counting silently, the ball rotating over the gray concrete. It crossed the three-meter mark and he stopped the timer. He looked at the screen. Two seconds.

"So how fast was it?" Anis asked.

Cole did the division on the back of his hand with the chalk. The ball had gone three meters in two seconds, so each second it had covered one and a half meters. "One point five meters per second," he said. "That's its speed. Three meters, two seconds, one point five."

"That's it? It looked way faster."

"That's the average," Cole said. He wrote the numbers on his hand: 0 seconds, 0 meters; 2 seconds, 3 meters. At home he would connect the two points and the slope of the line would be the speed. A steeper line would mean a faster ball, a flatter line a slower one, and the line for this ball sat exactly where the math put it, not where his eyes had.

Emerson rolled the ball again, and this time Cole called the numbers out loud as he clicked the stopwatch: "Three meters, two seconds, one point five." The chalk on his palm had already begun to blur, so he pressed his hand flat against his notebook before it could fade.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Pasta releases starch into its cooking water, and a splash of that starchy water helps a sauce thicken and cling to the pasta.
story:
The sign on the diner door read CLOSED, but inside Mr. Chatterjee's kitchen, everything was hot and loud and moving. "Fifty minutes," Mr. Chatterjee announced, tapping the big clock above the stove. "The food critic arrives at six, and my sauce cook called in sick. You three wanted a real job? Here is your real job." Declan rolled up his sleeves. So did Nora and Khalid, though Khalid looked like he was rolling them up for a funeral.

Declan's first task was the onions. He gripped the knife somewhere between confidently and dangerously, and Mr. Chatterjee slid a cutting board toward him. "Claw grip," he said, curling his own fingers like a bear paw. "Fingertips tucked, knuckles forward. The knife respects knuckles. It does not respect fingertips." Declan curled his hand into a claw and pressed the onion with his knuckles while the blade whispered past them. "I feel like a very cautious crab," he said, and Nora snorted so hard she almost dropped a garlic clove.

While the onions sizzled, the sauce went wrong. Declan had crushed the tomatoes, added the garlic, and let it bubble, but it looked thin and sad, like soup that had given up on life. Worse, it refused to stick to anything. He drizzled some over a test noodle and watched it slide right off into the bowl. "The critic will write that our sauce has commitment issues," Khalid said, poking at it.

Then Declan noticed something. The pot of pasta next to him had a cloudy, almost slippery look to the water, and when he fished out a spoon and let it cool, it felt faintly gluey between his fingers. Pasta releases starch into its cooking water, he thought, and starch was the thing that made sauces thick, wasn't it? He remembered his aunt's gravy going lumpy from flour. Maybe the water itself could do a job like that. "Don't dump that pot!" he shouted, just as Khalid lifted it toward the sink. Khalid froze mid-lift, like a statue of a man betraying his friends. "A splash of that starchy water helps the sauce thicken and cling to the pasta," Declan said, ladling a bit in and stirring. Nora saved a whole cupful, "in case of emergencies, or in case you're wrong."

He was not wrong. Within a minute the sauce turned glossy and smooth, and when he dragged another test noodle through it, the sauce clung on like it never wanted to let go. Khalid changed his mind about the whole plan with dramatic speed. "I take back every doubt," he declared. "You are a pasta genius. I am merely a pasta apprentice."

At 5:58 the plates went out. The critic, a small woman with a large notebook, twirled her fork, took one bite, and closed her eyes. Mr. Chatterjee peered through the pass-out window, gripping the counter. When the critic finally wrote something down, she held the notebook up so they could read it. Three words: "Sauce. Perfect. Again?"

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, objects of the same real size, like lampposts along a street, are drawn smaller and closer together the farther away they are.
story:
Hunter had until tomorrow morning to make his street drawing look like a street instead of a flat wall, and the lampposts were winning. He had five of them across the page, each exactly the same height, standing in a neat row like fence posts. He stared at the sketch at the kitchen table, then at the reference photo Ms. Demetriou had handed out, then back at his page.

"If they're the same height in real life, why do they look like that in the photo?" he asked Elie, who sat across the table working on her own version of the assignment. She leaned over and squinted at his lampposts. "In the photo they shrink," she said. "And they get squished together, kind of. Like they're huddling for warmth." Hunter grabbed a ruler and held it against the photo, measuring each lamppost. He had never tried to quantify a drawing before, but numbers felt safer than guessing. The closest one measured tall. The farthest one barely cleared the ruler's first mark, and the gaps between the posts shrank the deeper into the picture they went.

He remembered Tuesday then, the day Ms. Demetriou had drawn the street on the whiteboard while the class was supposed to be quiet because the refugee family visiting from the front office was being introduced down the hall. She had drawn one dot in the middle of the board and called it the vanishing point, and every line of her street had leaned toward it like it owed the dot money. Hunter had been half listening, doodling what he later told Elie was "definitely a snake and not a squiggle." Now he wished he'd paid more attention, because the snake was not going to save his grade.

"One-point perspective," he said slowly, tapping his pencil on the blank part of his page. "So all my lines go to one point, and the lampposts shrink toward it too." He erased his fence-post row, drew a small dot in the center of the page, and fanned faint lines out from it. Then he drew the nearest lamppost big and bold, and each one after it smaller and squeezed closer to its neighbor. Elie watched him work, chewing the end of her marker. "If you fail this," she said, "I'm telling everyone the snake was venomous and it distracted you. Self-defense. Very tragic."

"It was a squiggle," Hunter said, "and squiggles are harmless." He held the page up to the kitchen light. The street ran away from him, deep and real, the little posts marching toward the dot and shrinking the whole way, and for the first time all night it looked like somewhere you could actually walk. Elie leaned over, nodded once, and said, "Okay, now draw the snake on the corner. The street deserves it."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Grief can affect the body as well as feelings, often causing tiredness, trouble sleeping or changes in appetite.
story:
The toast sat untouched on Brooke's plate for the third morning in a row, and last night she had stared at the ceiling until the numbers on her clock read 2:47. She pressed the back of her hand to her forehead like her grandmother used to do. No fever. She wasn't stuffy, either, and her throat didn't hurt. So why did she feel like her bones were made of wet sand?

At school, Elly slid her tray across the table in the cafeteria. "You didn't eat your granola bar again," Elly said. "That's the whole week, basically." Brooke shrugged. "I keep thinking I'm coming down with something, but I can't find any symptoms." Mr. Otieno, who was on lunch duty, must have overheard, because he told her the nurse's office was open if she wanted to check in. He added that the nurse couldn't give out so much as a cough drop without a parent authorizing it first, but she could talk.

The nurse's office smelled like soap and paper towels. A small pamphlet rack stood by the cot, and while Brooke waited, she read the titles out of curiosity. One booklet was called When Someone Dies. Inside, one sentence caught her and wouldn't let go: grief can affect the body as well as feelings, often causing tiredness, trouble sleeping, or changes in appetite. She read it twice. Three things, and she had all three. She checked them off against herself like a scientist tallying data. Tired: yes. Trouble sleeping: two forty-seven in the morning, yes. Appetite: the toast, the granola bar, yes.

If that was the cause, then it wasn't a virus, and it couldn't be measured with a thermometer, like the sensor in the hallway smoke detector that beeped when it couldn't see clear air. This was something happening in her that no instrument could catch. She thought of a night last summer at Grandma's house, when the moon had come through the kitchen window so luminous on the floor that they'd turned off the lamp and eaten ice cream by moonlight alone. Grandma had said it was the best lighting in town and it was free.

That evening, Brooke put a photo of Grandma on her nightstand, just to test an idea. She ate half the toast, then the other half, slowly, tasting it. She asked herself whether grief might work like weather, something that arrived, did what it did, and eventually moved on. Sleep still came late, but it came.

In the morning, she slid the photo into her backpack to show Elly, and zipped it snug against her lunch.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Laughing along with teasing, even just to fit in, signals approval to the person teasing and tends to encourage them to keep going.
story:
On the second day of canoe camp, Ms. Morales announced that a storm was imminent, so the whole group had to haul the boats out of the water before the first fat raindrops landed. Charlotte was helping flip a canoe over when she heard the joke. "Nice paddling, Kyra," said a boy from the other cabin. "You steered us straight into the reeds like a human propeller." A knot of kids laughed, and Charlotte laughed too, a small snort she almost didn't notice making.

Kyra went red and pretended to be very busy with a paddle strap. The boy tried another joke, then another, each one a little meaner, and Charlotte noticed something odd. After every joke, he didn't look at Kyra. He looked at the laughing group, quick as a bird checking a feeder. It was like he wasn't really performing for Kyra at all. Charlotte started to wonder whether the laughs were the actual fuel, and whether the jokes would stall out without them. There was one obvious way to find out.

The next morning the sky was clear and the water was so flat it looked like a mirror that hadn't woken up yet. The boy drifted over to the dock where Kyra was untangling a rope. "Need help? Or are you going to tie yourself to the propeller again?" Charlotte, standing with Annabel nearby, kept her face perfectly still, like a person watching paint dry. Annabel glanced at her, caught on, and studied her shoes instead. The boy waited. The silence stretched out so long that a loon called somewhere just to fill it.

He tried again, louder. "I said, tie herself to the..." Annabel shrugged. Kyra, to everyone's surprise, said, "Ropes are actually hard, want to learn the knot?" That was worse for him than any insult. He mumbled something about going to find his water bottle and left at nearly jogging speed. "Did you see that?" Annabel whispered. "He kept checking if we were laughing. We stopped and the whole thing just died." Charlotte felt a grin spread across her face. "It's like teasing is a campfire. Take away the audience and you isolate the flame. No fuel, no fire."

Kyra walked over holding the untangled rope like a trophy. "So are you two going to teach me this knot, or just stand there looking smug?" "Smug," said Charlotte. "Definitely smug," said Annabel, and Kyra laughed so hard she dropped the rope in the lake and had to fish it out with a paddle.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when anxiety is intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life, a doctor may diagnose an anxiety disorder, which is treatable.
story:
The waiting room smelled like hand sanitizer and old magazines, and Alicia kept her eyes on the clock above the reception desk. School started in fifty minutes. If they weren't called back in the next ten, she would miss the bus, and her mother would have to drive her, and her mother had already driven her twice this month.

"Why are you so twitchy?" whispered Cian, who had come along because his own appointment was right after hers. He flipped through a magazine about wind energy, stopping at a picture of a giant white turbine on a hillside. "Look at this thing. It's taller than the school."

"I'm not twitchy," Alicia said. But her hands were folded so tight her knuckles had gone pale, and her stomach had that hollow, rolling feeling again. It had come every morning for three weeks now, always before school, always gone by lunch. She had started keeping a list in her notebook: what she ate for dinner, what time she went to bed, whether her stomach hurt the next morning. That was her idea. If she could find the pattern, she could fix it.

"You should ask Mr. Whitaker to postpone the science quiz," Cian said. "He does stuff like that."

"It's not the quiz." Alicia ran her finger down the page of her notebook, and then she stopped. Toast on Monday, hurt. Soup on Tuesday, hurt. Pizza at Eliot's on Wednesday, hurt. On Saturday, the same toast, the same pizza, and nothing. It wasn't the food. It was only ever school mornings. Something she couldn't see was doing this, and she was looking straight at the shape of it.

The door clicked open and a nurse called, "Alicia?" and her mother stood up, and that was when the twisting feeling jumped into her throat. Behind her, she heard Cian say quietly, not to her, almost to the magazine, "That's how it started with my sister. The stomach stuff." Alicia turned around. "What do you mean?"

"She thought it was the cafeteria food," Cian said. "It was anxiety. Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but hers was so bad for so long it got in the way of everything, so the doctor said it was an anxiety disorder." He shrugged. "It's treatable. She talked to the doctor about it, and now she's way better."

In the exam room, the doctor asked why she had come in, and Alicia's mother started to say, "Stomachaches, we thought maybe something she's eating," and Alicia heard herself say, "Can I go first?" She showed the doctor her notebook, all her careful columns, and pointed at the empty Saturday rows. "I tested the food idea and it's wrong. It's only school mornings. Every single one. Could it be anxiety?"

The doctor looked at the pages for a long moment, then back at Alicia, and pulled her chair closer. "That's good detective work," she said. "Let's talk about it."

"Alicia," her mother said, "why didn't you tell me?"

"Because I thought it was just stomachaches," Alicia said. Then, quieter: "And because I thought I was supposed to just cope with it."

"You don't have to just cope," the doctor said. "That's what we're here for." She tapped the notebook, still open to Alicia's neat rows of dinners and bedtimes, and the clock on the wall showed they had already missed the bus.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Each operation has an inverse that undoes it: subtraction undoes addition, and division undoes multiplication.
story:
Muhammad slid his worksheet across the table at the tutoring centre, hoping the problem would somehow evade him the way the smell of pencil shavings evaded everyone else. It didn't. x + 7 = 12 sat there in bold print, and under it, 5x = 35. He had missed the lesson on equations because he'd been home sick with a fever, and now the whole page looked like a tsunami of letters and numbers about to crash over him.

"You look like you're guarding a secret," said Laura, dropping into the seat beside him. She was there every Tuesday, and her actual reason for coming was the opposite of Muhammad's dread: she wanted to be the first in her class to finish the algebra booklet, because her older sister had framed hers and hung it in the hallway. She wanted a frame too. She leaned over his paper. "Oh, those are easy. Well, once you see the trick."

"Then tell me the trick," Muhammad said, but Marius, who was folding a paper airplane two seats down and listening more than he let on, spoke first. "It's not a trick, it's like locked doors. My dad changes the locks every year and keeps the old keys."

Laura rolled her eyes at Marius, then turned back to Muhammad. "Think about it. Somebody added seven to your x. What undoes adding seven?"

Muhammad stared at the equation. Something added. To undo it, take it back off. "Subtracting seven?"

"Subtraction undoes addition," Laura said, nodding. "And going the other way, division undoes multiplication. That's the whole booklet, basically." She tapped the second problem with her pencil. "So try your idea. See if it works."

Muhammad subtracted seven from the left side, then, remembering what she'd said about doing the same thing to both sides, from the right side too. x = 5. He checked it in his head: five plus seven really did make twelve. On the next one, 5x = 35, someone had multiplied x by five, so he divided both sides by five. x = 7. Five times seven, thirty-five. He felt like he'd found the old key after all, the one that still fit the lock.

When Ms. Lombardi came by to collect the worksheets, she paused at Muhammad's page, all six problems correct, and gave him a small nod before moving on. Marius launched his paper airplane and it swooped low over Muhammad's head, and Muhammad, feeling frugal with nothing but time now, picked up the next booklet from the stack. "What's this one called?"

"Two-step equations," said Laura. "Bring it over. I'll race you."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Streaming video uses far more mobile data than sending text messages, so watching videos away from Wi-Fi can use up a data plan quickly.
story:
The phone store smelled like new plastic and hope, and Katherine stood at the counter while her mom signed the papers. "Two gigabytes a month," the cashier said, sliding the box across. "Plenty, unless you stream a lot."

"That's what Vihaan said before his plan died," Janice whispered beside her. "Remember Tuesday?"

Katherine did remember, though it had been months ago, before she had a phone at all. Vihaan had slumped onto the gym bench holding his dark screen like a dead fish and announced that his data was gone in one week, all from watching videos on the bus every morning. At the time she had laughed. Now she clutched her own box a little tighter.

The first week was heaven. She texted Janice forty times, took photos of the neighbor's suspicious cat, and helped mediate a fierce argument between Janice and Vihaan about whose turn it was to pick the game at recess. Texts, photos, calls. Then, on the school bus, she got bored and opened a video of a raccoon opening a jar. Then another. By Thursday she was watching a whole series about a talking toaster, one episode per pothole.

On Saturday morning, her phone refused to load anything at all. She stared at the little bars at the top, full of signal, and yet nothing worked. She thought about Vihaan on the gym bench. Texts had cost him almost nothing, all month. Videos had cost him everything, in a week. It wasn't the phone, and it wasn't the signal. It was the plan itself, used up, and she could prove which part had eaten it.

She borrowed her mom's phone and sent Vihaan a message: "Emergency. Did you text a lot the month your data ran out, or mostly watch videos?"

"Videos," he wrote back. "Bus videos. Why?"

"Same. Bus videos. I have to survive until the first of the month."

Vihaan replied with a strategy that had clearly been hard-won: "Download episodes at home on Wi-Fi. Then the bus is free. Also the toaster series gets weird in episode six, so you're not missing much."

Janice, hearing the whole plan at recess on Monday, held up her own phone. "An anonymous number called me twice last night and hung up. I think it's the toaster people." Katherine snickered until Ms. Do, monitoring the lunch line, gave them the look that meant quiet, but with a small smile underneath it.

That afternoon, in the store's little service alcove below the office of the building's other tenant, a dentist, Katherine asked the cashier one careful question: "So videos away from Wi-Fi are the expensive part, and texts barely count?" He nodded, and she set a rule for herself, three downloads at home, zero videos on the bus, and wrote it on a sticky note for the phone's case.

Four weeks later, on the last day of her plan, her phone still loaded everything, and she stood at the bus stop holding it up like a trophy as Vihaan climbed on. "Still alive," she said, and pressed play.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: In a healthy onion cell, the cell membrane is pressed tightly against the inside of the cell wall, which makes the membrane very hard to see as a separate line.
story:
Theodore's pencil hovered over the diagram, stuck on the third blank. He had found the cell wall easily enough, a thick dark outline around every brick-shaped cell, and the nucleus sat in the middle like a small gray dot. But the worksheet said to label the cell membrane too, and he could not find it anywhere.

"Maybe onions just don't have one," Reid said from the next stool, not even looking up from his own microscope. "That's my answer. Drawing an arrow to nothing."

"That's not an answer, that's giving up," Theodore said. Dax laughed without lifting his head. The three of them had been assigned the same slide, a whisper-thin layer of onion skin stained purple, and Ms. Ross had told them their diagrams were due before the bell. Theodore adjusted the fine focus, scanning the edge of one cell. One line. Only one line. If there were a membrane, shouldn't it look like a second line, just inside the wall, like a fence inside a fence?

He thought about last week, when he had wrecked his first slide by cranking the stage up too fast and cracking the coverslip. Ms. Ross hadn't scolded him; she had just said, "The lens is closer than you think, Mr. Theodore. Most things you break, you break because you can't see the distance." He had been careful ever since, and that memory was what made him stop and think now instead of guessing.

Maybe the membrane was there, just closer than he thought. Pressed right up against something. He turned the light adjustment down until the field dimmed, and the thick wall went soft and pale. Then, at the very inner edge of the wall on one cell, a single faint line appeared where the wall was, no second line beside it, no gap, nothing separate. He turned the light back up. Gone. He did it again. There.

"Look," he said, grabbing Reid's sleeve. "Dim your light and watch the edge of a wall."

Reid squinted. "I still only see one line."

"Exactly. In a healthy onion cell the membrane is pressed tight against the inside of the wall, so you can't see it as its own line. It's there. It's just hiding against the wall." His heart was going fast, the way it did when a math problem cracked open all at once.

"So how do I label it?" Reid asked.

"Same arrow as the wall. Point to that edge and write both."

Reid actually did it, then held up his worksheet. "If you're wrong, we're both wrong."

"You two realize grading isn't subjective, right?" Dax said, not looking up. "There's a right answer. Ms. Ross prescribed the exact labels on the sheet. Wall, membrane, nucleus. This isn't art class."

"It's not wrong if we can defend it," Theodore said, and raised his hand. "Ms. Ross? Question about the membrane."

She came over, and Theodore pointed at the dim circle of light under his lens. "We could only find one line. The membrane's pressed against the wall, so it isn't a separate line in a healthy cell. Is that right?"

She leaned down, looked, and straightened up. "Label it on the edge, then, like you told your friend there. Nice work." She moved on toward the window row, where someone had knocked over a beaker.

Reid wrote his arrows slowly, tongue between his teeth. "First one I've gotten right all semester," he said. "Don't tell Dax I said that."

"I heard it," Dax said. "It's going in the history books. Reid's diagram, the start of a whole dynasty."

"Then label your dynasty carefully," Theodore said, and dimmed the light one more time to check.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Practicing in several shorter sessions spread over days usually builds a skill better than the same total time crammed into one long session.
story:
Savannah had three measures of "Ode to Joy" left to learn before Friday's assembly, and the clarinet in her hands still squeaked on the high F like an angry duck. Mr. Nikolaidis had posted the sign-up sheet for the assembly on Monday, and her name was on it, in her own handwriting, which suddenly felt like a terrible decision.

"You sound like a dying goose," said Phillip, who sat two chairs over and never let anyone forget he had played since third grade.

"Thank you," said Savannah. "Very helpful."

Esteban leaned across his music stand. "How much did you practice this week?"

"Two whole hours. Last night." She held up her reed case as proof, as if the worn reed could testify for her. "I played that F at least a hundred times and it still squeaks."

Esteban frowned and turned his own trumpet over in his hands. "I only practiced twenty minutes a day this week. Total, that's less than your two hours." He lifted the trumpet and played his whole solo line, clean, every note landing where it belonged.

Savannah stared at him. The same total time, spread differently, and his notes came out right while hers squeaked. She turned the idea over the way she turned the clarinet keys, testing whether it was really solid. If it was true, then one long desperate night was the wrong tool entirely, and several shorter sessions spread across the days would build the skill better. She thought about the bake sale the band had run in October, how the income from it had paid for the new music stands only after weeks of small sales adding up, not one giant day. Small amounts, spread out, did the work.

That afternoon she found Mr. Nikolaidis stacking chairs and petitioned him to open the music room before school for the rest of the week. "Voluntary practice," she said. "Just for anyone who wants twenty minutes of quiet. I'll unlock it myself if you sign the form."

He raised an eyebrow. "Twenty minutes?"

"Twenty minutes, every morning, until Friday."

He signed. On Tuesday morning she played the F forty times and it squeaked thirty-nine of them. On Wednesday it squeaked twenty-two times. On Thursday morning, Phillip wandered in with his flute, pretending he had just happened to be early, and played his part beside her. The room filled with the sound of two imperfect instruments learning to be less imperfect together.

Friday morning, twenty minutes before the assembly, Savannah stood at the window with the clarinet assembled and the reed wet. She breathed in, set her fingers on the keys, and played all three measures through, slow and even. The high F came out round and clear, and Phillip lowered his flute long enough to mutter, "Finally."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: The Gunnery camp, begun in 1861 by Connecticut schoolmaster Frederick W. Gunn, who led his students on a hike to a camp by the sea, is usually considered the first organized American summer camp.
story:
The camp handbook had been sitting on Raphael's desk for three days, unopened, while he packed. Now it was six o'clock, the van left at seven, and he had a duffel bag whose contents were roughly proportional to its importance, which meant the flashlight was buried under four extra T-shirts nobody would ever see him wear.

Nikita arrived with a bag of chips and no luggage of his own, which seemed unfair. "You're going to a month of bad cuisine," he said, crunching. "Beans from a pot. Beans from a different pot."

"It says here there's a cook." Raphael had finally opened the handbook, mostly to avoid the flashlight excavation. A page near the front had a short history of the place, and a photo of a plaque by the lake. He read it twice. "Huh. It says the Gunnery camp started in 1861. This Connecticut schoolmaster, Frederick W. Gunn, took his students on a hike to a camp by the sea. It's usually considered the first organized American summer camp."

"So?"

"So I thought camps were invented, like, forty years ago by people who hated children. This thing's older than Canada." He checked that. It was. "You're telling me some guy in 1861 decided a hundred and whatever students should walk to the ocean and sleep outside, on purpose, and now I have to do it too."

Nikita peered at the plaque photo. "That contradicts my whole theory of camps."

"Which was?"

"That they were punishment." Nikita ate another chip. "Your theory is also that. You packed like it's punishment."

Raphael looked at the duffel. He had packed for a disaster, not for a month by a lake. The 1861 guy had hiked to the sea with, presumably, less than four extra T-shirts. Raphael tested a simple idea: if camp had worked since before his grandmother's grandmother, the bag did not need to contain everything ever manufactured. He dumped it out. The flashlight rolled under the bed, which felt like a sign.

At seven, his father honked. Alena ran over from next door with a ziplock of cookies and a note card. "For the bus," she said. On the card she'd written "1861" and drawn a little hiker. "You said the schoolmaster guy hiked to the sea. First one ever to do the whole thing."

"I'm not the first one ever to do anything," Raphael said, hauling the lighter bag.

"You're the first Raphael at that camp," said Alena.

From the van window, he waved the note card like a ticket, and his father pulled out before Nikita could say anything about beans.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: At 5 percent simple interest, $1,000 earns $50 a year, so after five years the account holds $1,250.
story:
Nevaeh slid the birthday card across the kitchen table and read the note inside for the third time. Her grandfather had written that he would hold her one thousand dollars for five years at 5 percent simple interest, and that she should figure out for herself what that meant. "Figure it out," she muttered. "Thanks, Grandpa."

She called Neil first, because Neil loved money the way other kids loved dinosaurs. "A thousand dollars," he breathed into the phone. "You could buy the new racing game, the headset, AND the controller with the extra buttons." That was Neil's whole plan for her money, of course, since his own allowance had gone extinct two weeks after he spent it all on stickers. "But what happens if you just leave it with your grandpa?" she asked. Neil yawned. "Nothing happens. Money just sits there."

That answer bugged her all through dinner, so after dinner she excavated her notebook from the bottom of her backpack, where it had been buried under three old permission slips, and started doing math. If five percent meant fifty dollars for every hundred, then a thousand dollars earned fifty dollars in a year. She wrote it down: year one, one thousand fifty. Year two, one thousand one hundred. She kept going, adding fifty each time, until year five ended at one thousand two hundred fifty dollars. Two hundred fifty dollars for doing nothing. Neil was wrong, and she couldn't wait to tell him.

The next morning she found Ms. Nikolaidis on her porch, sorting mail. Ms. Nikolaidis was the kind of neighbour who had opinions about everything, including the weather, which she called corrosive to her garden fence. Nevaeh laid out her numbers and asked the question that had kept her up. "Is there a way money grows faster than that? Like, if the interest got added in and then the whole bigger amount earned the next fifty?" Ms. Nikolaidis tapped the paper. "That's compound interest, dear, and yes, banks do that. Your grandfather's way is simple, the same fifty every year." Nevaeh stared at her own handwriting. So the fifty could stack on top of other fifties somewhere else. Somewhere, money was doing that without her.

She ran two blocks to Neil's house and knocked until he opened the door in his socks. "Two hundred fifty dollars," she announced. "After five years I'll have one thousand two hundred fifty. That's the deal." Neil leaned against the doorframe. "So buy the game now, have fun now." Nevaeh shook her head slowly. "If I wait, I get the game AND two hundred fifty dollars. That's like the game paying me to wait." Neil squinted at her, and she could almost hear the gears grinding.

At school on Monday, Nevaeh cornered him by the lockers with a new page of math. She had spent Sunday trying compound interest with a calculator, and the five-year answer came out bigger than one thousand two hundred fifty, though she still wasn't sure she'd pressed the buttons right. "I'm going to ask my mom about a real bank account," she said. "One where the interest compounds." Neil sighed the sigh of a boy watching a fortune slip away, then held out his hand. "Fine. But when you're rich, I get one snack." Nevaeh shook it. "You get half a snack."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Laundry is sorted by colour because new dark or bright clothes can release dye into the wash water, and that dye can tint white and pale clothes.
story:
Gavin had never thought much about laundry until Mr. Njoroge announced a life-skills week and wheeled a washing machine into the classroom like it was a game show prize. "By Friday," Mr. Njoroge said, "each of you will run a full load, start to finish." Gavin's mom was going to be thrilled. She'd been telling him for a year that he could learn this at home, and for a year he'd been responding by lying very still on the couch.

Kayden dumped a bin of practice clothes on the table. There were towels, gym shorts, a stack of white school shirts, and one bright red sock so new it still had a tag on it. Bianca started making piles immediately, darks in one, whites in another, her lines running parallel like parking spaces. Gavin figured one big pile would save time, so he shoved everything in together, added soap, and pressed start before anyone could stop him.

Forty minutes later, the white shirts came out pale pink. Not dramatic pink. Not flamingo. Just a soft, sneaky, uniform pink, like a sunset had leaned on them. "What did you do," Bianca said, holding one up to the light. Gavin stared at the red sock, which had come out of the machine looking completely innocent. He had a theory forming, and it felt a bit like being a detective, except the suspect was footwear.

He ran a test. He filled a clear bowl with warm water and dunked the red sock in it all by itself, no shirts allowed. Within a minute, the water had a faint red haze drifting through it, like smoke trapped under glass. The sock was letting dye loose into the water. That had to be it. The dye went into the wash water, the water went everywhere, and the white shirts soaked it up. New sock, new dye, and the tag still on it. Gavin felt his brain make a small clicking sound.

"So the pink shirt was the water's fault," he announced. "The dye got into the water, and then the water shared it with everything. Like a bad group project." Bianca snorted. Kayden proposed a treaty: he would stop hiding Gavin's sneakers if Gavin never mixed a load again. Gavin shook on it, then folded the pink shirts into a neat stack and carried them to Mr. Njoroge's desk like evidence.

Mr. Njoroge held one up, raised an eyebrow, and said, "Nice fold."

"Check the water bowl," said Gavin. "I caught the criminal red-handed. Well. Red-socked."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors, a process called peer review.
story:
Dad had barely finished serving the noodles when Mom slid her phone across the table. "Look at this," she said. "A man froze his batteries for a day, and they lasted three times longer in his remote. I already put the new ones in the freezer."

Brooke chewed slowly. One man, one remote, one time. That didn't sound like much of anything, and tomorrow she was supposed to hand in a current science topic to Mr. Weber, a real one, with a source that would not fall apart the second someone looked at it. This might be her chance to solve both problems at once.

"Can I test it?" she asked.

Mom sighed the sigh of a woman who had already bought the batteries. "Fine. But don't use the good remote."

That afternoon Brooke sat in the library with Lianna and Maria, two identical remotes on the table, one battery fresh from the freezer and one from the drawer. While they waited for something to happen, Lianna pushed a journal article across the table, one she had found for her own topic. It was about battery performance, and it was dull, dense, and full of charts. Next to it lay the blog post Mom loved, which had exclamation points. Maria frowned. "Why does this one look so much more official?"

"Before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors," Lianna said, tapping the article. "It's called peer review." The blog, as far as any of them could tell, had been reviewed by nobody except the man's enthusiasm.

The test itself took all evening. Brooke set the two batteries upright in identical remotes, turned the volume up on both, and taped the buttons down so each one drained at the same rate. She arranged them on her desk perpendicular to each other so she could tell them apart in the dark, then checked every twenty minutes and wrote down the times. The frozen battery died at 9:42. The regular one died at 9:51. Nine minutes. Barely a shrug.

At dinner the next night she brought the notebook, the remotes, and both articles. Dad reached for the bread just as she opened to her data table, which she suspected was his version of an escape plan.

"Nine minutes," she said. "That's it. And the journal article, the one where actual experts checked it before it got published, tested way more batteries than two and found basically nothing."

"So the freezer was a waste of space," Mom said.

"The freezer was a waste of space. The blog was one guy who probably had a good battery to start with."

Dad grinned. "Should I tell your grandmother her ice-cube diet is next on Brooke's list?"

"Dad. Do not embarrass me in front of the data." She slid the peer-reviewed article toward Mom, who put down her fork and started reading the charts, pausing only to take the batteries out of the freezer.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Japan's Obon festival, held in mid-August in most regions and in July in some, honors the spirits of ancestors, who are believed to return home for a visit.
story:
Christopher's grandfather had died in June, and the apartment still felt wrong in small ways. His chair at the table was empty. His crossword pen sat in the jar by the phone, and nobody moved it. Christopher wanted to do something, anything, that would make the goodbye feel finished, but he couldn't figure out what.

On the first Sunday of August, Aksil called from Japan. He was staying with his grandparents' neighbors in a town outside Kyoto, and the video connection made his face wobble. "It's Obon here," Aksil said. Christopher asked what that meant. "It's a festival," Aksil said. "Mid-August in most regions, July in some. The spirits of ancestors come home for a visit."

Christopher sat up straighter. "Home. Like, here?"

"Like wherever home is," Aksil said. He turned the phone toward the window, and Christopher saw paper lanterns glowing along a street, small orange moons in a row. Aksil's voice came back close to the speaker. "We lit one for my grandmother. First Obon without her."

That night Christopher lay awake reasoning it through. He couldn't see a spirit arrive. Nobody could. But if the whole thing worked on a rule, spirits returning during the festival, then the lantern was the part you could test. If the rule was real, a lantern at his own window should count as home too. Grandpa had lived in this apartment for nine years before he moved to the care home. If any place was home, this was it.

On Monday he found Curtis at the park and tried to summarize the idea out loud, because saying it to someone made it more real than thinking it. "It's like a door," Christopher said. "The festival is when the door is open, and the lantern is how you say which door is yours." Curtis scratched his chin. "So build one. You could use that contemporary lamp kit from science club, the one with the LED and the paper shade." Christopher hadn't thought of that. He'd been picturing candles, which his mom would veto in about two seconds.

They built it in Christopher's kitchen. Curtis held the paper cylinder while Christopher taped the seam, and the LED inside made the whole thing glow warm yellow, close enough to the lanterns in Kyoto. His mom came home while they were testing it and didn't veto anything. She stood in the doorway with grocery bags still in her hands and looked at it for a long moment. Then she went to Grandpa's crossword pen and set it beside the lantern on the sill, as if it belonged there.

At school Ms. Bouchard had them write short research pieces that week, and she reminded everyone that facts needed a citation, the place where you found them. Christopher wrote about the festival and put Aksil's call down as his source. Ms. Bouchard read it, then read it again, and asked him quietly if the lantern had worked. Christopher said he didn't know yet. The festival days in his region were mid-August, and that was still a week away.

On the night in the middle of August, he set the lantern in the window facing the street. He turned it on and sat on the floor beside it with the crossword from that morning's paper, Grandpa's pen in his hand. He filled in one across answer, 7 Down, then 22 Across, and left the rest of the grid blank on purpose, the way they used to do when they ran out of time. The little light glowed steadily against the dark glass. Down on the street a car passed, and then it was quiet, and Christopher whispered, "The door's open."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A reverse image search can show where a photo appeared online before, which can reveal that an old picture is being passed off as new.
story:
Raphael climbed onto the bus holding his phone like it was evidence in a trial, which, in a way, it was. Amar was already in the third row, leaning across the aisle to show Diego a photo of a brown river swallowing a street. "Downtown's under water," Amar said. "My cousin posted it. School's definitely closing."

Raphael sat down and scrutinized the picture. Water to the top of a stop sign, a kayak paddling past a mail truck. It looked dramatic. It also looked, somehow, already seen, the way a joke you've heard twice does. "When did your cousin take this?" he asked.

"She didn't. She shared it." Amar was optimistic about floods the way some kids are about snow days; a disaster was just a day off with better scenery. "It says breaking news right on it."

"Anyone can type breaking news," Raphael said. "That's an opinion with a font."

Diego frowned. "So it's fake?"

"I didn't say fake. I said nobody's checked it." Raphael knew the difference now, because Ms. Paquette had spent one entire Tuesday on it: some things you could only argue about, and some things you could actually look up. Whether downtown was flooded was the second kind. He copied the image, opened a search engine, and pasted it in. Amar watched over his shoulder, breathing loudly, the way people do when they want the answer to be yes.

The results loaded. The same kayak, the same mail truck, the same stop sign, on pages that were years old. "Wait," Diego said. "What did you just do?"

"Reverse image search," Raphael said. "It shows where a photo appeared online before." Which, in this case, was everywhere, and years ago. Amar took the phone and scrolled, his day off dissolving one result at a time. He handed it back without a word.

"So my cousin shared an old picture," Amar said finally. "She didn't know."

"She could check it the same way I did," Raphael said. "Forward her the link."

The bus hissed around the corner by the senior residence, where two old men sat on the dry porch arguing over a crossword. Amar was already typing to his cousin, thumbs going fast. "If there's ever a real flood," Diego said, "how will we know?"

Raphael pocketed his phone. "Same way," he said. "We'll look."

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: One complete time through the twelve bars is called a chorus, and a soloist often plays several choruses in a row.
story:
The church basement smelled of dust and coffee, and the folding chairs had been pushed against the walls to make room for the music ministry's Saturday practice. Violet sat on a metal chair with her trumpet on her lap, watching Ms. Pham count off the band. Three weeks ago, when she had first wandered down after the Sunday service, she had only wanted somewhere to practice that wasn't her thin-walled apartment. Now she was being asked to solo.
