"Blues in B flat," said Dominik, who played keyboard and seemed to know everything. "Twelve bars, then it starts over. One time through all twelve bars is a chorus." He said it the way he said most things, quickly, like he was handing her a pencil.

The chord progression was invisible. That was the problem. Nothing in the room showed her where the music was except Dominik's left hand, and he moved it too fast. She had missed her entrance twice already because she counted bars the way she counted pages in a book, and somewhere between bar four and bar five her mind drifted into the arid stretch of the progression where every bar sounded the same to her ear. She could hear the chords, but she could not see the shape underneath them.

She thought back to math class, to the unit on ratios. Twelve bars, she remembered thinking, was like a ratio of chord to bar, three chords spread over twelve bars, and if she tapped her foot the whole time, every twelve taps meant she had traveled the whole shape once and landed back at the beginning. On her last try she had tested it, tapping quietly against the chair leg, and when her count reached twelve, Dominik's hand had jumped back to the same chord as before. The pattern was real. It circled.

"When Violet's ready, she takes two choruses," Ms. Pham said, tapping her music stand twice.

Two choruses. Twenty-four bars. Violet stood, raised the trumpet, and the cold mouthpiece touched her lips. She stopped thinking about notes and started thinking about the shape, the invisible circle she was traveling. The band propelled her forward through the first chorus, and she let a few notes spill out, low and cautious, then climbed a little when the progression climbed underneath her. Somewhere around bar nine, her stomach tightened, but her foot kept tapping and her count held. Twelve. The circle started over, and she heard Dominik's hand jump back to the first chord exactly when she expected it.

The second chorus braver, she bent one note the way the saxophone player had bent his, a small curved sound that surprised her. She reached bar twenty-four and stepped back from the microphone. The basement went quiet except for the hum of the old refrigerator in the corner.

"That," said Dominik, "was two whole choruses."

Violet grinned and wiped the mouthpiece on her sleeve. "Can I have three next time?"

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut, because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house.
story:
The lights went out just after Beatrice set her homework on the kitchen table, and the whole farmhouse went quiet in a way it never did in daylight. The hum of the refrigerator stopped. The clock over the stove went dark. She heard her grandmother's chair scrape in the living room, then footsteps feeling their way along the hall.

"Power cut," her grandmother called. "I'll get the candles."

Beatrice sat still for a second, listening. Outside, the wind pushed against the barn and the power lines swayed where she knew they ran along the road, though she could not see any of it. That was the thing about a dark house, she thought: the cause of the trouble was out there somewhere on those lines, invisible, and she could only guess at it from the sound of the wind. Her mind did the same trick in reverse when she tried to picture the fuse box in the cellar. She knew its shape, its cold metal door, but not what had tripped inside it tonight.

"Wait," she said, standing up and finding the counter by memory. "Don't light those." She remembered Mr. Goldberg, who had come to her class back in the spring with a crate of safety gear. He had not given a lecture. He had held up a flashlight in one hand and a candle in the other and let the class argue about which one belonged in a power cut. Beatrice had argued for the candle, because it seemed braver, and she had been wrong. Safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut, she had copied into her notebook, because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house. It had felt like a paradox at the time, the thing that made light also being the thing that could burn the place down.

Her grandmother was hesitant at the hall closet, matches already in her hand. "Candles got us through forty years of storms, Bea."

"I know. But we have three flashlights in the drawer by the sink." Beatrice bumped her hip on a chair, apologized to it out loud, and slid the drawer open. Her fingers found rubber grips, cold and certain. She clicked one on and the kitchen reappeared, pale and smaller than she expected. She clicked the second one and handed it over.

Her grandmother turned the flashlight over in her hands, studying it the way she studied a new calf. Then she blew out the match she had been saving and set the candle box back on its shelf, high and out of reach.

"Good girl," she said. "Go see if the one in the mudroom still works."

Beatrice padded to the door, swept the beam across coats and boots, and found the third flashlight tucked behind the umbrella stand. She thumbed the switch, and a thin circle of light landed on the window, where the wind was still busy with the wires she could not see.

"There you are," she said.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In W. W. Jacobs's 1902 story The Monkey's Paw, Sergeant-Major Morris warns that the paw's wishes bring terrible results and throws it into the fire before the family rescues it.
story:
The book club met in the back corner of the library, where the radiators ticked and the window looked out on the arid stretch of gravel behind the parking lot. Luke had read "The Monkey's Paw" twice, and he still couldn't say what the paw was supposed to mean. Jordan could. Jordan had written a whole page about it.

"Okay, my turn," Jordan said, flipping his notebook open. "The paw is a symbol. It stands for greed, or maybe fate, and the fact that it's a monkey's paw means humans are grabbing at things that aren't meant for them."

Ms. Sandhu nodded slowly and looked around the circle. "Anyone want to build on that or push back?"

Luke looked down at his copy of the story. He had circled three places where he'd felt something odd in the wording, though he couldn't have said why. "There's the part where the sergeant-major throws the paw in the fire," he said. "Before anybody even makes a wish. I kept thinking that had to mean something."

Nada sat forward. "That's foreshadowing. He's warning them."

"He's literally warning them," Luke said. "It's not even hidden. Sergeant-Major Morris says the wishes bring terrible results, and then he throws the paw into the fire, and the dad goes and grabs it out anyway." He tapped the page. "So the story warned everyone before the first wish was ever made. Whatever happens after that, we can't say we didn't see it coming."

Jordan frowned at his notebook. "So then the symbol is... the fire? Fire is supposed to cleanse stuff, and the dad thwarted that by rescuing the paw."

"That works," Nada said. "Or the paw itself is the warning, and they just ignore it."

Luke tried an idea out, the way you test a loose tooth. "Maybe that's the trick of it. Foreshadowing isn't the author whispering. Sometimes a character just comes out and says it, and the scary part is nobody listens." He read the line aloud, the one about the man who wished for death, and the room went quiet enough that they could hear the radiator tick three times.

Ms. Sandhu smiled. "That's a claim worth writing down, Luke. Can you defend it with two more moments from the text?"

Luke flipped pages, hunting for his circled spots. "Give me a minute," he said. "I know they're in here somewhere."

Jordan slid his pen across the table. "Use mine. Ink, not pencil."

"Thanks." Luke started to write, then stopped. "Wait. The chess bit at the beginning. The dad loses at chess because he takes a risky move. That's it, that's the other one. Everything in this story is somebody taking a risk they were warned about." He underlined it twice, and the pen made a small satisfying scratch against the paper.

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: Ohm's law is named after the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm, who published it in 1827.
story:
Autumn sat cross-legged under the climbing dome with a battery pack, a coil of thin wire, and her brother's multimeter, which she had borrowed without asking and felt slightly vulnerable about, since he counted it among his treasures. Elena hung upside down from the bars above her, watching.

"You said the science fair was in two weeks," Elena said. "Why are we at the playground?"

"Because the garage smells like gasoline and my mom keeps asking if I need help." Autumn clipped the wire to the battery and touched the multimeter probes to each end. "Watch. 6.0 volts." She unclipped one probe and moved it so the current meter sat in the loop instead. "0.4 amps."

"So what does your mystery wire do?"

"That's the thing. I can't see resistance. It's inside the wire, like a hidden property. But if voltage pushes and current flows, I can infer it." She wrote 6.0 divided by 0.4 on the back of her hand and got 15. "Fifteen ohms."

Elena dropped down beside her. "Ohms. Like the name?"

"That's what I wondered. Why would a unit of electricity have a person's name?" Autumn flipped through her notes. Mr. Weber, her science teacher, had written one sentence on her proposal sheet: Ohm's law is named after the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm, who published it in 1827. She had circled it twice.

"A German guy figured out the rule before the Civil War," Autumn said. "Almost two hundred years ago. So the unit got his name."

"That's the irony," Elena said. "He's famous for something invisible."

Autumn tested it. Her idea was that a longer wire should have more of that hidden resistance, so she clipped in twice the length and measured again: still 6.0 volts, but now 0.2 amps. She divided and got 30. Double the length, double the resistance. The rule held.

Francesca arrived with a slushie and peered at the setup. "You're doing homework at a playground."

"It's not homework, it's detective work," Autumn said. "I'm hunting something I can't see by looking at what it does to things I can see."

Francesca squinted at the numbers. "I thought science fair projects had to have explosions or volcanoes."

"I thought so too," Autumn said. "I was going to do the baking-soda volcano. But this is better, because nobody built a volcano in 1827 and got a rule named after them." She wound the extra wire back onto its spool and wrote the heading for her poster: The Hunt for the Hidden Number.

Elena swung back up onto the bars. "Fifteen ohms!" she called down. "Invisible and famous!"

Autumn packed the multimeter into her backpack, zipped it, and ran for the swings.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Children and teenagers should not take aspirin during flu or chickenpox, because it is linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious illness affecting the liver and brain.
story:
The pharmacy closed at nine, and it was already twenty past eight when Paisley's mother dropped her at the door with a crumpled ten-dollar bill. Paisley's head still ached from the flu, her throat felt like sandpaper, and the fluorescent lights made everything buzz a little. Somewhere between the cough syrup and the vitamins she found the shelf of pain relievers, and she began to coordinate her three needs in her mind: her headache, her fever, and the ten dollars, which would not stretch to everything.

She reached for the aspirin first, because it was the cheapest and the box looked conventional, the kind of thing her grandmother kept in her kitchen drawer. Then she flipped it over and squinted at the fine print on the back. The label said not to give it to children or teenagers during flu or chickenpox, because it was linked to something serious. She read the line twice. Her ears were blocked and hot, and the small letters seemed to swim.

"Ms. Martínez?" she croaked, waving toward the pharmacist at the counter. "This aspirin box says kids shouldn't take it with the flu. But it doesn't really say why. Is it just a rule for little kids, or me too?"

Ms. Martínez came around the counter and looked at the box, then at Paisley's red nose. "It's linked to a rare but serious illness affecting the liver and brain," she said. "It's called Reye's syndrome."

Paisley stood very still while the words sanked in. Rare, but serious. Liver and brain. She was eleven, which meant she counted as a child, and she had the flu right now, which meant the warning applied to her exactly, not to somebody else. She thought of the bottle of aspirin sitting in her own bathroom cabinet at home, the white pills her mother sometimes handed out for headaches. Her mother might not have read the back of that bottle in years. Old bottles probably had old labels, and old labels might not carry the warning at all.

"Can I borrow your phone charger?" Paisley asked. "Just for a second. My phone's dead." At the outlet by the photo machine, she plugged in, waited through the longest thirty seconds of her life, and called home. "Mom, don't take the aspirin from the cabinet for me. Not while I have the flu. Get the acetaminophen, the blue box, second shelf." Her mother asked why, and Paisley said, "It matters. I'll explain when I'm back."

She bought the acetaminophen with four minutes to spare and pushed through the doors into the cold night air, where the wind on her feverish face felt, from her droopy perspective, almost wonderful. Her mother's car idled at the curb, and through the window Paisley could see the blue box already sitting on the passenger seat, held out like a prize.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Many museums ask visitors not to touch objects, because oils and salts from skin build up over time and can stain or damage the surfaces.
story:
The bus dropped Alice's class at the nature reserve just after nine. Mr. Mercado handed out maps and read the day's plan aloud: a hike on the ridge trail in the morning, and after lunch, a tour of the old ranger station, which had been turned into a small museum. Alice folded the map into her pocket and followed Tabitha toward the trailhead, where Leanna was already waiting with a water bottle in each hand.

The hike was fine until Leanna twisted her ankle on a loose rock half a mile in. Mr. Mercado wrapped it and let her sit on a fallen log while the rest of the group continued to the overlook. When they came back down, Leanna held out her phone. "I wrote you a note," she said. "Since I can't walk fast, read it when you do the tour." The message said: "Look for the secret. There's a place in the ranger station where a hundred years of hands left a mark. Find it and tell me what it is."

Alice was hesitant to leave Leanna on the log, but Mr. Mercado promised to stay with her, so Alice joined the line into the ranger station. Inside, the guide pointed out the old wooden desk where the first ranger had written his reports, and a wooden railing that ran along the entry hall. Behind her, a boy in a red jacket reached out to drag his hand across the desk's surface. Tabitha caught his wrist. "Don't. Museums ask visitors not to touch things because oils and salts from skin build up over time and can stain or damage the surfaces." The boy pulled his hand back and wiped it on his shorts.

Alice thought about what Tabitha had said all the way down the hall. Oils and salts from skin. Build up over time. She stopped at the railing and looked at it closely. The rest of the wood was dull and grey, but the top of the railing, exactly where a hand would grip it, was dark and slightly shiny in a smooth band. She put her face close without touching. The shine ran the whole length, at hand height, and nowhere else.

She turned around and walked back to the desk. It sat behind a rope, but she could see the same thing on its edge: a dark patch on the front lip, right where a person would rest a hand while sitting. She raised her hand. "Is that dark spot on the desk from people touching it?" The guide nodded. "That's the hand print of every ranger who ever worked there, one on top of another."

After the tour, Alice hiked back up the trail fast enough to make her lungs burn. She found Leanna on the log, finishing the sandwich that was meant to consume the last of her appetite before the ride home. "It was the railing," Alice said. "A hundred years of hands left a shine on it, and the same mark on the desk." Leanna grinned and tapped her phone. "I already took the picture. Look."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Wool shrinks in hot, sloshing water because tiny scales on each wool fibre open up and lock onto neighbouring fibres, pulling the knit tighter. This is called felting.
story:
The 42 bus was late again, and John sat on the bench with a paper grocery bag between his knees. Inside was the sweater, folded as flat as he could make it, which was not very flat.

"What's in the bag?" Luc asked, dropping onto the bench beside him.

"Evidence," John said. "Of a crime I committed."

Philemon leaned over from the other side. John peeled the bag open. Luc pulled out the sweater, held it up, and stared. It was small enough for a doll, its cables puckered and stiff, its sleeves hardly longer than thumbs.

"Whose is that?" Philemon asked.

"Mine. My grandma knit it for me last winter. It came down past my hips." John took it back and turned it over in his hands. "Saturday was my first time doing a whole load by myself. Mom's got her arm in a sling, so it was me or nobody. I sorted the darks from the lights, checked pockets, everything. Then I shoved it all in on hot, because hot water has to be better, right? More hygiene. More cleaning power."

Luc winced. "And?"

"And I came back after the spin cycle and found this." John held the sweater up again. "Everything else was fine. The towels were great. Only the sweater turned into this."

The bus appeared at the far corner, then vanished behind the bakery, which meant it wasn't the 42. Philemon tossed a pebble at the curb. "So hot water shrinks sweaters. Mystery solved."

"That's what I thought," John said. "But then I got curious. I ran a test." He pulled a scrap of paper from his pocket, a list written in pencil. "I took a square of the same yarn from grandma's leftover ball and washed it in cold, gentle water. It barely changed. Then I tried a square in hot water in a bucket, but without sloshing it around. Also almost fine. It was the hot water plus the moving that did it. Hot and still, no. Cold and sloshy, no. Hot and sloshy, tiny doll sweater."

Luc frowned. "That makes no sense. Water isn't alive. How does water know?"

"That's what I couldn't figure out," John said. "I called my grandma. She wasn't even mad, which was worse somehow. She said every wool fibre has tiny scales on it, and in hot, sloshing water the scales open up and lock onto the neighbouring fibres, pulling the knit tighter and tighter. She said it's called felting."

"Felting," Philemon repeated, as if testing the word. "So the sweater grabbed itself smaller."

"Basically the whole sweater shrank itself," John said. "Nobody did it to it. It did it to itself." He looked down at the ruined cables and thought about the months of knitting, the arid weeks of January when he had worn it every single day to the bus stop, this very bench, pulling the collar up against the wind.

"So you're taking it to her to fix?" Luc asked.

"She says she can't undo it. But she said she'd teach me to knit, and I could make something new out of the felt. A mitten, maybe." John shrugged, then straightened. "Actually, I already started. Last night I did the cast-on row four times until it worked. And I've done two loads of laundry since, both cold, both fine."

Philemon grinned. "So next Saturday you'll be the laundry expert and a knitting apprentice."

"Grandma says experts elaborate. Apprentices just have a lot of wool."

The 42 rounded the corner at last. John stood, tucked the little sweater back into the bag, and shouldered his backpack. "Tell your moms," he said, stepping onto the bus, "cold and gentle for anything knit."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In February 2015 a photo of a dress went viral because some people saw it as blue and black and others as white and gold; the real dress was blue and black.
story:
Mason slid his phone across the dinner table the moment his father sat down. "Look at this dress. What color is it?"

"White and gold," his father said, without even putting down his fork.

Mason turned to his mother. She leaned over, squinted. "Blue and black. Obviously."

"Obviously?" His father set down the fork after all. "It's white. With gold lace. I'm looking right at it."

Mason looked at the same screen and saw blue and black, same as his mother, which was strange because his father was the one in the house who noticed everything, like the day the neighbor moved her mailbox three feet to the left. His father did not miss things. Yet here he was, calmly describing a completely different dress.

Mason had a plan. He texted Mathieu, who lived two streets over and would answer anything, and then Edmund, who would answer anything but wrongly. Mathieu replied in nine seconds: white and gold, are you blind? Edmund replied: blue and black, why do you even ask. That made it two against two, and the four of them had looked at the same photo on four different screens. So it wasn't the screen. He turned his brightness up and down and held the phone at arm's length. His father still said white and gold. His mother still said blue and black.

"Maybe you're all messing with me," Mason said.

His mother put her hand on her chest, wounded. "I would never. That is blue."

"It is white," his father said, with the patience of a man being reasonable at a lunatic.

Mason needed more evidence. He walked next door and rang Mr. Adebayo's bell, holding the phone out before the door was fully open. Mr. Adebayo studied it, then laughed. "This again. My whole family split over that thing in February. My brother threatened a household amendment, no dress talk at dinner. Half the internet fought about it, you know."

"And the actual dress?" Mason asked. "The real one, in a store."

"Blue and black. There's a photo of it somewhere. It went viral because everybody saw it differently."

Mason walked home slowly, turning this over. He had assumed there was one right answer and one wrong one, and that the wrong one belonged to his father. But his father wasn't wrong about what he saw. He was wrong about the dress, but right about the white and gold, if that made any sense at all. Maybe it didn't have to.

At the table, his parents were still going. His mother had pulled up the photo of the real dress, royal blue with black lace, and his father was leaning in with narrowed eyes, like a man approaching a legitimate court exhibit.

"Huh," his father said.

"That's an apology," his mother said.

"That's a 'huh.'"

Mason set his phone face down between the salt and the green beans. "New rule. We vote on something we can actually settle. Like whether Edmund counts as a reliable witness."

"Edmund," said his mother, "is the boy who told you gummy bears grew on trees until fifth grade."

"He retracted it," Mason said, and passed the potatoes.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted.
story:
On Saturday morning Christopher stood at the gate of the community garden holding a paper bag of gloves that Ms. García had handed him, wondering what he had agreed to. Behind the vegetable beds, volunteers were sorting crates of tomatoes, carrots, and slightly bruised apples into boxes marked for the food bank distribution table. His friend Emerald waved him over to the sorting station, where a boy named Mathias was pulling soft oranges out of a crate one at a time.

"These came from the grocery store on Fifth Street," Emerald said. "They donate the stuff that looks weird, or that didn't sell fast enough. Apples with bumps. Carrots with two legs." She held up a carrot that split like a pair of scissors at the bottom, and Mathias laughed so hard he dropped an orange.

Christopher picked up the orange and turned it over. It was a little soft on one side, but the rest felt fine. "If a whole store gives away this much," he said, "how much never gets eaten anywhere? Like, everywhere in the whole country?" He was already trying to work out how you'd even count that, since nobody could see all the food in America at once.

Mathias shrugged, but Emerald pulled out her phone. "My mom made me memorize a fact for the food drive poster at school," she said, and scrolled through her pictures. She turned the screen around. In big green letters it said the U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted.

Christopher stared at the number. "That's like four out of every ten apples just gone," he said. He glanced at the crate of soft oranges, then at the line of neighbors already forming at the distribution table near the gate. Maybe the pile in front of him wasn't the whole story. Maybe most of the wasted food never even made it to a garden like this, and what he was seeing was an illusion of plenty. He wanted to know if the soft oranges could still be used, because if they could, that was a small piece of the problem he could actually fix.

"Ms. García," he called, "could we cut around the soft spots instead of throwing these out?" She said that would be feasible if they had enough knives and cutting boards, so Christopher asked Mathias and Emerald to collaborate with him on a trimming station. Ms. García found three plastic knives, and soon they were carving good halves out of bad oranges while neighbors at the table picked up the pieces in little bags. A woman with a stroller took four halves and said her kids loved oranges but she never bought the ugly ones because they cost the same as the pretty ones.

By noon the crate was empty except for peels, and Christopher felt his legs aching from standing. Then Ms. García came over holding a clipboard and a strange look on her face. "I called the store to thank them," she said. "Turns out they've been donating for two years, and nobody ever told us they had a whole cold room of bread and eggs in the back. They thought we couldn't handle it." She set the clipboard down. "Would you three be willing to come back next Saturday with a van?" Christopher looked at Emerald, who was already grinning, and at Mathias, who raised his plastic knife like a sword. "We'll be here," Christopher said, and he pulled the gloves back out of the bag.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Friendships usually fade without contact, so friends who move apart and stay close tend to keep in touch regularly through calls, messages or visits.
story:
The morning after the moving truck left, Everly sat in a classroom where every desk had a name tag except hers. Mr. Charles handed her a blank tag and a marker, and she wrote her name in block letters while twenty-eight students watched. He pointed to an empty seat beside a girl with braids, who slid her pencil case over to make room.

At lunch the girl, Adelina, asked where Everly had lived before. "Fairview," Everly said. "My best friends there are Margaux and Priya." Adelina said the equivalent of that at her old school had been two boys she'd known since kindergarten, but when her family moved last spring, she never heard from them again. "It's like we just stopped existing to each other," she said. Everly pushed her tray around and thought about that all through afternoon math.

That evening she called Margaux, who was sorting comic books into boxes. Everly had an idea and she wanted to test it. "Adelina lost her old friends because they moved and nobody kept in touch. So let's do the opposite. Every Sunday at four, video call. If we do it regularly, we stay close. That's the whole plan." Margaux said her mother would never let her miss it if it were on the calendar, so they made it official and wrote it on the wall planner in orange marker.

The first Sunday, Priya joined too, and they all drew the same dragon from a tutorial, comparing results on camera. The second Sunday, Margaux's internet went out, so she called from the library and held her phone up to a book about fantasy, which was the only genre all three of them read. Everly began to incorporate pieces of Fairview into her new life, telling Adelina the jokes Margaux made and showing her the drawings Priya sent.

By October, Everly noticed a pattern in Adelina. Adelina texted her cousin in another state every single day, and that cousin was still her closest friend. But Adelina's old neighbor had moved two years ago, there had been no calls, no messages, no visits, and now Adelina couldn't remember the neighbor's last name. Two friendships, two different results, and the difference was contact. Everly wrote it in her notebook like a science observation, then felt silly and crossed it out.

In November, Mr. Charles assigned a project on communities, and Everly chose to survey students about friends who had moved away. She asked one question: do you still talk to them, and how often? Out of nineteen answers, the eleven students who called, messaged, or visited their old friends said they were still close. The other eight mostly shrugged.

The day before winter break, Everly's Sunday call came through with snow falling behind Margaux's window. Priya held up a painted figure and said, "Next week you're drawing with us, no excuses." Adelina leaned into the frame from the couch beside Everly and waved.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The U.S. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13, which is why many sites require users to be 13.
story:
Isla sat cross-legged on Emmitt's bedroom floor while he dumped a bag of chips between them and passed her his phone. "You have to see Marisol's video," he said. "She posted the science fair volcano exploding and it has, like, two hundred comments." The app was called Flicker, and Isla had been wanting an account ever since the whole group chat started moving there. She tapped Sign Up.

The first questions were easy. Username, password. Then a white box appeared: Date of Birth. She typed her birthday, September 14, and the phone buzzed and the screen went gray. A message in small print said accounts could not be created for users under 13. "That's weird," she said. "I'm twelve. My birthday's in two weeks."

Emmitt leaned over her shoulder, breathing chip smell onto her cheek. "Just lie," he said. "Nobody checks." Isla stared at the box. She could type anything, and the phone would believe her. But something about it snagged in her mind, the way a thread catches on a nail. She scrolled down and found a long page of rules nobody ever reads, and near the middle was the answer: a law, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998, said websites had to get parental consent before collecting personal information from children under 13. That was why so many sites made you say you were 13.

"So they ask your birthday," she said slowly, "because if you're under thirteen, the whole app would be too invasive. They'd have to call your parents first." Emmitt shrugged. "Then put thirteen. Marisol did it, I bet. Everybody does it." He was already back to watching the volcano video with the sound turned up, the plastic hiss of bubbles almost real through the speaker.

Isla started a little experiment. She cleared the form and typed a birthday that made her twelve years and ten months old. Gray screen. She tried twelve years and eleven months. Gray screen again, the same flat buzz, like the phone was shrugging her off. She tried thirteen years exactly. The screen bloomed green, and suddenly there was a place for her profile picture, her interests, her school. The app wanted to invest her in it right away, little prizes for filling in every blank. Her thumb hovered.

Down the hall, a door opened, and Ms. Li called, "Emmitt, is Isla staying for dinner?" Emmitt yelled back something with his mouth full. Isla looked at the green screen, then at the blank where it asked for her school, her real name, her city. Two weeks, she thought. In two weeks she'd be thirteen and it would all be true anyway. She pressed the back arrow until the form disappeared.

"Forgot my password," she told Emmitt, and slid the phone across the carpet toward him.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal.
story:
Alexis slid a crumpled flyer across the dinner table so his father could see it. "The game convention is Saturday, and there are only two hundred holographic Dragonheart cards, and one kid at school is selling his for forty dollars." He had saved twenty-two dollars from raking leaves, which had felt like a fortune until this week.

His father stirred his soup and looked at the flyer. "Forty dollars for a card. You know what we paid for water today? A whole case of bottles for three dollars." He held up his glass. "You can't live without water, but it's cheap. A tiny diamond costs thousands and nobody needs one to survive."

"That's weird," Alexis said, chewing slowly. He thought about that instead of the card for a moment. "Water does everything, and it's almost free. A diamond just sits there." He remembered Ms. Lawson mentioning something like this in class on Tuesday, so after dinner he dug out his notes. There it was, underlined twice: In The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal. So people had noticed this puzzle almost two hundred fifty years ago, and it was still true at his own dinner table.

The next morning he found Celina at her locker and told her the whole thing. "Ms. Lawson talked about it, remember? Adam Smith, 1776, The Wealth of Nations." Celina laughed and said, "Only you would turn a card into homework." But she frowned at the flyer thoughtfully. "So if everyone wants the card and there are only two hundred, the price goes up. Like the diamond. If there were a million of them, it would cost as much as water."

"Exactly. So the price isn't about how good it is. It's about how many there are compared to how many people want one." Alexis decided to test it. He made a small poster for his locker: TRADING DRAGONHEART? MEET ALEXIS. By Friday, three kids had offered theirs, and the lowest price was eighteen dollars. He bought that one, keeping four dollars to spare, and felt like he'd solved something.

At Saturday's convention he spotted Ainsley near the entrance staring at a display case with a frail, hand-drawn banner sagging over the table. A canopy of balloons swayed above the vendors, and beneath it Ainsley pointed at a glass box. "Look. The card's in there. Signed by the artist."

Alexis leaned closer. There were thirty identical cards fanned out under the glass, each one holographic, each one signed, and the sign above them read: TEN DOLLARS EACH, LIMIT TWO PER PERSON. He looked at his card, then at the case, then at the empty space in his wallet where eighteen dollars used to be. Ainsley grinned and said, "I'd hurry. There's already a line."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: In a fire, smoke and heat rise, so the cleaner, cooler air is near the floor, which is why firefighters teach people to crawl low under smoke.
story:
Samuel wedged his knee against the seat in front of him and studied the worksheet Mr. Sutherland had handed out on the bus. The field trip was to the fire station, and the whole visit would run on a tight schedule: one hour, then back on the bus, because the firefighters had a real call drill at eleven.

"Question six is impossible," said Zackery, leaning over the aisle. "It says, 'Why would you crawl instead of run in a smoky hallway?' I put 'because you'd trip.'"

Nimrit, who sat by the window with her binder open on her knees, tapped her pencil against question six. "My cousin's a firefighter. She says something about the air down there. I can't remember what."

Samuel turned his pen sideways and rolled it between his fingers. He was thinking about the fog machine from the school haunted house last October. The haze had hung at the top of the gym first, thick and gray, and only later had it settled. Everyone said the machine was broken, but maybe it wasn't broken at all. Maybe that was just what smoke did. If the air near the floor was cleaner and cooler, because smoke and heat rose upward, then crawling wasn't about tripping at all. He scribbled a draft answer and covered it with his hand. "I've got a guess," he said. "But I want to check it before the bus gets there."

The bus rattled over a pothole, and Mr. Sutherland stood up at the front. "When we arrive, the station will accommodate us in groups of ten," he said. "Booths, gear, and a practice tunnel. And yes, you may bring your worksheets."

At the station, a firefighter in a helmet that looked too big for him showed them a display case. "This jacket has a polymer barrier in the lining," he said. "Keeps the heat out." Zackery poked the glass and asked if the boots had polymers too, and the firefighter laughed and said pretty much everything did.

Then came the tunnel. It was a long canvas corridor, and a harmless smoke machine filled the top of it with an opaque gray haze, so thick Samuel couldn't see the exit sign above it. The firefighter knelt at the entrance. "Stay low, move slow, and follow the wall."

Samuel got on his hands and knees beside Nimrit. Just under the haze, the air was clear enough that he could see all the way to the bright rectangle at the far end, and it felt cooler down there, away from the warm fog overhead. He turned his head. "It's cleaner down here," he said. "That's why we crawl. The smoke and heat rise, so the good air is near the floor."

"Write it down before you forget," Nimrit said, and she pulled her binder off her back and slid it along the floor in front of her.

Zackery crawled behind them, knees squeaking on the canvas. "My answer was still kind of right," he said. "I would totally trip."

They spilled out the far end into the truck bay, and Mr. Sutherland checked his watch. "Four minutes to finish question six, then we board." Samuel braced the worksheet against his knee, wrote three quick sentences, and passed his pen back to Nimrit.

"Your turn," he said.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is thinned with water while wet, but once it dries it becomes water-resistant, so brushes must be washed before the paint dries on them.
story:
Jordan lined up his supplies on the kitchen table like a general preparing for battle: five brushes, a jar of water, and the poster board for Ms. Nwosu's classroom mural audition. Lennon had left the brushes at the studio overnight, and now Jordan picked one up and tried to bend the bristles. It wouldn't bend. All five were stiff as sticks, the bristles fused into hard little points.

"Did you leave these in water?" Jordan asked when Lennon arrived, cheeks flushed from running the whole way over.

"No, we got kicked out at five," Lennon said. "Benoit spilled paint on the floor and Ms. Nwosu made us mop."

"So the paint dried on them overnight." Jordan held a brush up to the window and turned it slowly, thinking. He dipped it in the jar of water and swirled it hard. Nothing happened. The dried paint stayed rock solid, and the bristles stayed stuck together. That told him something important: once acrylic dried, water couldn't touch it.

"Soap?" Lennon suggested.

"Water and soap both have water in them," Jordan said. "It's not going to work." He tried anyway, scrubbing the brush against his palm, and the bristles only bent at the tip like a broken twig.

Lennon started to perspire, wiping his forehead with his sleeve. "Then we're doomed. The audition is at three. We can't paint a mural entry with fingers."

Jordan wasn't listening. He was reasoning backward. If dried paint was water-resistant, then wet paint had to be the opposite, thinnable, washable. Which meant a person had to wash brushes while the paint was still wet on them. The brushes hadn't been washed wet. They'd been abandoned wet and left to dry. So the damage was already done. Unless.

"Test something for me," Jordan said, grabbing the one brush he'd brought home himself. He squeezed a blob of blue acrylic onto a plate, dragged the brush through it, and painted one aggressive swooping stripe across a scrap of paper. Then, before even setting the brush down, he plunged it straight into the jar. He swirled. He pulled it out. The bristles were soft, clean, spread out like new.

Lennon actually cheered. "It's the timing! Wash them wet and they survive!"

"That's the rule," Jordan said, laying the ruined brushes aside for the trash. "We use my brush, and we never let paint dry on it. Not even for a minute." He set the jar of water directly beside the poster board, close enough to reach without standing up.

Benoit arrived at the door ten minutes later, holding a plastic bag. "I found two more brushes in the supply closet," he announced. "Also, my hands are completely blue and it won't come off."

"Didn't wash them wet, huh?" Jordan said, grinning as he uncapped the paint. "Sit down. Grab a brush. Rinse it the second you're done, every single time." He pressed the brush to the corner of the poster board and drew the first curve of a rising wave.
